definition.text: Extinction is the end of a species, reached when its last member dies.

facts.text: A species can be functionally extinct before its last member dies, if the few survivors can no longer reproduce and recover.
More than 99.9% of all species that ever lived are extinct, and the average species lasts 1–10 million years.
Habitat degradation is currently the main human cause of extinctions, and agriculture is the main cause of habitat degradation worldwide.
Humans have become an extra cause of extinction, both as a new mega-predator and by moving animals and plants around the world.
Fossil studies confirm extinction caused by climate change; a 2003 review predicted 15–37% of land species would be 'committed to extinction' by 2050 because of climate change.
There have been at least five mass extinctions in the history of life on Earth.
A 2014 special edition of Science declared a widespread consensus that humans are driving mass species extinctions.
Because the moment of extinction is hard to pin down over a large range, it is usually decided after the fact.

definition.text: Coextinction is the loss of one species because another species it depends on has gone extinct.

facts.text: Parasitic insects can die out after their hosts are lost, and predators can vanish when their prey or a plant its pollinator disappears.
It is especially common when a keystone species goes extinct.

definition.text: Genetic pollution is uncontrolled interbreeding with introduced or hybrid populations that swamps a native species' gene pool.

facts.text: It most threatens rare species that come into contact with abundant ones, whose hybrids deplete the pure gene pool.
The endangered wild water buffalo is most threatened by genetic pollution from the abundant domestic water buffalo.
Such extinctions may not be visible from an animal's outward appearance.

definition.text: A Lazarus taxon is a species or group thought to be extinct that is later found again.

facts.text: The coelacanth was known only from fossils and thought extinct since the end of the Cretaceous, until a living one was found off South Africa in 1938.
Such reappearances show how hard it is to establish exactly when a species has gone extinct.

title: De-extinction by cloning

definition.text: De-extinction is the proposal to bring an extinct species back to life by cloning it from DNA in its remains.

facts.text: Proposed targets include the mammoth, the thylacine, the dodo and the Pyrenean ibex, which has been cloned before.
Success would need enough clones from the DNA of different individuals to form a viable population.
It seems possible in theory, though bioethical and philosophical objections have been raised.
IUCN guidelines from 2016 hold that an extinct species cannot be perfectly recreated, so the results are called 'proxy species'.
It could restore lost ecological functions but carries risks such as disease transmission, hybridization and animal suffering.

contested_note: Critics see de-extinction as 'playing God' and a threat to animal welfare, while others defend it as restoring nature.

definition.text: Extinction debt is the future extinction of species that has already been set in motion by past events such as habitat loss.

facts.text: It arises from time lags: long-lived trees, for example, may survive for years after new trees can no longer be produced.
Habitat fragmentation and habitat destruction are its best-known drivers, because they cut off species' ability to recolonize other patches.
It is most likely in long-lived species and in specialists with narrow habitat needs.
The term was first used in 1994 by Tilman, May, Lehman and Nowak; it is likened to the 'climate commitment' of warming that continues after emissions stop.
Modelling of species–area relationships suggests 80–90% of the extinctions due to past Amazon deforestation have yet to happen.
In the Azores, where over 95% of native forest was destroyed in 600 years, more than half of arthropods are thought committed to extinction.
It means protecting today's habitat may not be enough, but the long delay gives time for habitat restoration to prevent losses.

definition.text: Extinction debt is detected by checking whether today's species better match past habitat than present habitat, or by comparing cleared and intact areas.

facts.text: It is hard to measure because the processes are slow and noisy and tiny remnant populations are hard to count, so estimates are very uncertain.
The size of the debt can only be estimated if past species populations are known as well as present ones.
In moss microcosm experiments, insect species took 6–12 months to die out after habitat was destroyed.
